The Verses of the Elder Aṅgulimāla:
“You say ‘I am going,’ yet you stand as a recluse;
and you say of me who am standing, ‘You are not standing.’”
“I ask you about this matter, ascetic:
‘How is it that you stand while I do not stand?
“I always stand, Aṅgulimāla.”
Having laid aside the rod toward all beings,
you yourself are unrestrained toward living creatures;
therefore, while I stand firm, you do not stand firm.
“After a long time, indeed, the Great Seer who was honored by me has entered the Great Forest as a recluse;
therefore, I shall renounce my thousandfold evil.”
Having heard this verse of yours connected with the Dhamma,
the robber thus cast away his sword and weapon into a pit,
a precipice, and a hellish abyss.
The thief bowed at the feet of the Sugata and right there requested ordination from the Buddha.
And the Buddha, the compassionate Great Seer—
To him who was the Teacher of the world together with its devas,
he then said, "Come, bhikkhu";
that itself became his state of being a bhikkhu.
But he who, having been heedless in the past,
is not heedless afterwards—
he illuminates this world.
Like the moon released from clouds,
he whose evil deed is covered over by a wholesome one—
He illuminates the world like the moon freed from clouds—
he who is indeed a young bhikkhu.
He applies himself to the Buddha’s teaching;
he illuminates the world like the moon freed from clouds.
May people in every direction hear my discourse on the Dhamma;
may people in every direction apply themselves to the Buddha’s teaching;
may people in every direction associate with those noble ones.
The virtuous indeed teach only those things that are wholesome.
For in all directions, there are those who speak of patience and praise non-opposition.
Let them hear the Dhamma at the proper time,
and let them act accordingly;
for he shall never harm me.
Or whatever else there may be;
having attained supreme peace,
one should protect both the timid and the steadfast.
For irrigators lead the water,
fletchers straighten the arrow,
and carpenters bend the wood.
The wise tame themselves.
Some tame [themselves] with a staff,
with goads, and with whips.
Without staff or sword,
I am tamed by suchness;
"The Harmless One" is my name.
Though formerly I was a hater,
today I am truly named "Truthful," for I do not harm anything whatsoever.
I was formerly known as Aṅgulimāla, O Sage;
I was being swept away by a great flood.
I have come for refuge to the Buddha.
Formerly, I was one with blood on my hands,
widely known as Aṅgulimāla.
Behold this going for refuge;
the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
Having performed such a deed,
Much [merit] leads to a miserable rebirth;
touched by the ripening of my karma,
I eat my food free from debt.
Fools of little intelligence devote themselves to negligence,
but the wise person devotes himself to heedfulness.
He guards it like his most excellent wealth.
Do not indulge in negligence;
do not cultivate intimacy with sensual pleasures.
For one who meditates with diligence attains supreme happiness;
it is well-come, not gone away.
This was not poorly considered by me;
among all analyzed phenomena,
I have attained that which is supreme.
It is well-spoken, not ill-spoken;
this was not poorly conceived by me;
the three knowledges have been attained.
This is the teaching of the Buddha:
in the forest, at the foot of a tree,
on mountains, or in caves.
I stood right there,
my mind then filled with anxiety;
yet I slept and stood in ease.
I live my life in happiness;
outside the reach of Māra, oh,
how I am compassionately cared for by the Teacher!
Formerly I was Brahmajāca,
a high-born man on both sides;
now I am the son of the Sugata.
Of the Teacher, the King of Dhamma.
Free from craving, without grasping,
with guarded doors and well-restrained;
Having destroyed the root of evil,
I have attained the destruction of the taints.
The Teacher has been served by me.
The teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled;
the heavy burden has been laid down,
and the conduit to existence has been uprooted.
